problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 4 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $M=PJ{P}^{-1},$ find $\operatorname{ln}⁡M.$

examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Value of a Function of a Jordan Decomposition
examples.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/17b4d68be43e4a4eb895ebbe623b713f1a808153424dd221b7497579d666b00a.png)

Given that $V = PJP^{-1},$ find $\sin\left(\pi V\right).$
examples.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SAS^{-1}) = S \cdot f(A) \cdot S^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x) = \sin(\pi x)$ and the given matrix $V,$ we have

$$
\sin(\pi V) = \sin\left(\pi{PJP^{-1}}\right) = P \cdot (\sin(\pi J)) \cdot P^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $J$ is a Jordan block with $-3$s on the main diagonal, we have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/a8ad3d4a15a5a8e7307fdd6449d8086d6c9c7e656caea877d41f021c7d8584cc.png)

The derivative of $f$ is $f'(x) = \pi \cos \pi x.$ So, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/9af57a3b00b9c9e64508c119ae77690904bdb8c30b124b8165d4280149361bad.png)

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14072904/assets/ff9333784a9cdd38f510398b48e485764eac400f56c2cc9f2f1a18e5138845d8.png)

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi V) & =P\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi J))\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -\pi  \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\pi  & -\pi  \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\pi  & -\pi  \\ \pi  & -\pi \end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.

|  |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} | {{field-3}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}))=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | {{field-4}} | {{field-5}} |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-6}} |  |
feedback.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡([\begin{aligned}{J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}))\end{aligned}] \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}))\,⊕\,\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})) & =[\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda =\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={sec}^{2}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =[\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3})\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{1}(\frac{\pi }{3}))\,⊕\,\operatorname{tan}⁡({J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
